To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Mexican-American women who are full‐time homemakers are more satisfied with discretionary family time, amount and type of work accomplished at the home and friendships than are women who are employed either full- or part‐time.

Mexican‐American women who are full- or part‐time employed are not less satisfied than full‐time homemakers with their family life, their quality of life, or their satisfaction with resource management, although some differences in specific areas of resource satisfaction were found.

Mexican-American wives are generally satisfied with their families and quality of life regardless employment status, and that homemakers are more satisfied with discretionary and leisure time and with their work and friendships than are employed wives.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the employment status of Mexican-American wives on their perception of resource availability and satisfaction with resource usage.
the effects of employment on family resource management.
the relationship between employment and family life, and it provides evidence that employment status is not the primary factor in determining resource use or satisfaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the employed wife is not necessarily less satisfied with resource management than the non-employed wife.
employment status is not an important determinant of satisfaction with family resources and quality of life for Mexican-American wives.
the employed wives were not less satisfied with their family lives than the non-employed wives.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
employment does not necessarily have a negative impact on the quality of life of Mexican-American wives.
employed wives were not disadvantaged in their use of family resources and in their quality of life compared with non-employed wives.
employed wives were more satisfied with the availability of resources, while nonemployed wives were more satisfied in their usage of resources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women's work is never done, and the work of the homemaker is no less important or valuable than the work of the employed.
the quality of life of Mexican-American wives is not necessarily enhanced by their employment status.
the quality of life of Mexican-American wives is not necessarily compromised by employment outside the home.
